fix_commit.message: Avoid a potential use-after-free in fts5. Report [bugs:/info/2026-06-08T08:45:27Z | 2026-06-08T08:45:27Z].
fix_commit.author: dan

findings.title: Use-after-free via buffer reallocation in fts5ExprNearIsMatch
findings.message: In fts5ExprNearIsMatch(), each phrase's lookahead reader is initialized with a raw pointer (reader.a) into the phrase's poslist buffer (pPoslist->p). The function then sets pPoslist->n = 0 and writes matching entries back into the same buffer via sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend(). That function internally calls fts5BufferGrow() which may invoke sqlite3_realloc() to grow the buffer. If reallocation occurs, the old pPoslist->p memory is freed, but a[i].reader.a still points to it. Any subsequent call to fts5LookaheadReaderNext() reads through the now-freed pointer — a use-after-free. The fix replaces sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend (which may reallocate) with sqlite3Fts5PoslistSafeAppend (which assumes the buffer is already large enough and never reallocates), eliminating the stale-pointer hazard. The bug can be triggered with trigram tokenization and a NEAR query against a document producing many overlapping trigram hits, causing the poslist buffer to need to grow during the write-back phase.
findings.suggestion: Replace sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend() with sqlite3Fts5PoslistSafeAppend() in fts5ExprNearIsMatch(). The safe variant writes directly into already-allocated space without calling fts5BufferGrow, so it never reallocates the buffer and the lookahead reader's pointer stays valid. The buffer is safe to write without growing because new poslist entries are always a subset of the original, so space is guaranteed.

ground_truth.root_cause: sqlite3Fts5PoslistWriterAppend() unconditionally calls fts5BufferGrow() before writing, which may reallocate the Fts5Buffer's internal data pointer. Because the lookahead reader for the same phrase was pre-initialized with the original pointer value, any reallocation frees the memory the reader is actively traversing. The design comment in the code states that in-place overwrite is safe because output is a subset of input (no bytes being written can overwrite bytes yet to be read), but this analysis ignores the possibility that the allocator may move the entire buffer to a different address.
